readerTitle: Who sells for you when you're not in the room?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (사무실 청소 회사, 지역 식품 브랜드와 슈퍼마켓 체인) · 모든 인물과 상황은 설명용
insight: 영업의 결정적인 대화는 내가 없는 방에서 일어난다. 그래서 나를 좋아하는 사람이 아니라, 그 방에서 나를 대신해 말해 줄 사람을 찾고 도와야 한다.
misconception: 고객사 안에서 나에게 가장 친절하고 열정적인 사람이 내 편이다. 또는 결정권자에게 직접 가면 내부 지지자는 필요 없다.

sources.text: B2B 영업의 일반 개념 (내부 지지자 champion: 영향력, 개인적 동기, 실제 행동으로 구분)
모든 인물과 상황은 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: 모든 사례와 인물은 가상입니다. 통계나 연구 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다. 카드에 특정 영업 방법론 이름(MEDDIC 등)은 넣지 않았습니다. 추가한다면 출처를 먼저 확인하세요.

cards.title: Who sells for you when you're not in the room?
body: The call went great. Your contact nodded and laughed. At the end she said, "I love this. I'll take it to my boss."
Two weeks later there is still no reply. The decision happened in a meeting you never saw. Someone spoke for you there, or no one did.

image.label: A closed meeting-room door with a proposal on the table inside
image.brief: 닫힌 회의실 문. 유리창 너머로 두 사람이 테이블 위 제안서를 보고 있음. 문 밖 복도에서 영업 담당자가 휴대폰을 들고 답장을 기다리는 모습. 따뜻한 일러스트 톤, 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Three people at the accounting firm.
body: You run an office cleaning company. You're bidding to clean a 200-person accounting firm. You've met three people:

**Dana**, the receptionist, is warm and complains about the current cleaner. **Mark**, the office manager, hears every complaint and reports to the director. He's polite but cautious. **Priya**, the operations director, signs the contract. You met her once. Who do you invest the most time in?

options.text: Dana. She's the most enthusiastic about switching.
options.feedback: Her support feels great, but she has little say in the decision. You gain a friend and lose weeks.

options.text: Priya. Go straight to the person who signs.
options.feedback: You need her approval, but she'll ask Mark what he thinks. Without him on your side, you're a stranger with a quote.

options.text: Mark. Help him see how switching makes his job easier.
options.feedback: He has access to Priya and a personal reason to want fewer complaints. If he believes in you, he'll argue for you in the meeting you can't attend.

cards.title: Liking you is not selling for you.
body: Many sellers pick Dana. She returns calls and says yes to everything. But her yes doesn't reach the meeting where the choice gets made.
Mark is harder work. He asks tough questions about cost and reliability. That caution is exactly why Priya trusts his view.
When Mark sits down with Priya, he either says "I think we should try them" or he says nothing. That one sentence often decides the deal.

cards.title: A champion
body: A **champion** is a person inside the customer's business who wants you to win and works to make it happen when you're not there.

A real champion has three things. **Influence:** the decision maker listens to them. **A reason:** your solution helps them personally, with fewer headaches, a target met or credit earned. **Action:** they actually do things for the deal.
A fan has only the third one in words. A champion has all three.

image.label: A 2x2 grid: influence versus personal reason to help
image.brief: 2x2 매트릭스. 가로축 "Personal reason to help", 세로축 "Influence". 오른쪽 위 칸 "Champion" 강조, 오른쪽 아래 "Fan", 왼쪽 위 "Gatekeeper", 왼쪽 아래 "Bystander". 칸마다 작은 인물 아이콘.

cards.title: Test with small asks, not compliments.
body: Kind words cost nothing. Small actions show you who is really helping. Ask for something and watch what happens:
list: Will they **introduce you** to the decision maker?
Will they explain **how the decision actually gets made** and who might object?
Will they share what their boss cares about most?
Will they forward your proposal **with a note of their own**?
cards.callout: A champion acts. A fan agrees.

cards.title: Make your champion look good.
body: Your champion has to sell you in their own words, often in five minutes. Give them what they need: a one-page summary, answers to the objections their boss will raise, and a clear first step with low risk.
Then make sure success shows up as *their* win. People argue harder for ideas that make them look smart.
cards.softwareNote: In software, the champion is often the team lead who ran the free trial. Give them usage numbers from their own team and a simple rollout plan they can present to the person who holds the budget.

cards.title: One champion is a single point of failure.
body: Champions change jobs, lose arguments and go on leave. If one person carries your whole deal, the deal leaves with them. Build trust with a second person over time.
Also, don't ask a champion to risk their reputation on a promise you can't keep. And don't go around them to their boss without telling them. You may win one meeting and lose your best ally.

cards.title: Now it's a grocery chain.
body: You make a regional hot sauce. One store in a 30-store grocery chain stocks it, and it keeps selling out. The store manager is thrilled. Stocking more stores is decided by a category buyer at head office.
The manager says, "I'll mention you to the buyer." What do you do?

options.text: Thank her warmly and wait for the buyer to call
options.feedback: She means well, but a passing mention is easy to forget. You keep her goodwill and give her nothing to use.

options.text: Skip her and cold-email the buyer with your pitch
options.feedback: You reach the decision maker faster, but as a stranger. The manager's results are your strongest proof, and you'd leave them out.

options.text: Send her a short summary of her store's sales and ask if she'd introduce you
options.feedback: You turn her enthusiasm into a specific action and hand her proof the buyer will respect. It also makes her look good for spotting a winner.

cards.title: Find the person who will speak for you, then equip them.
body: The most important sales conversation usually happens without you. Look for someone with influence, a personal reason to help, and a willingness to act.
**Try it today:** pick your biggest open deal. Write down who will speak for you when the decision is made. If you can't name anyone, ask your contact for one small action this week.
